text: She leaves a-- this woman leaves a full sack of grated cassava sitting in a corner for three whole days. You see, in this compound, garri is money. Whosoever reaches the market first on Friday sells first. Her family-- her husband's family grate, press, and fry on the same day. By evening, their basins are full. Hers, one sack tied tight under a heavy stone. Her mother-in-law doesn't whisper it. She said, "This is-- this one is not making garri. She's raising it." Every market day, they sell out before noon. She arrives on day three. She arrives on day three when the customers has gone home. Her garri is so-- there is... There is-- The whole compound agrees she's lazy. Then the rain failed to fall. One month, two months. The yams are gone. The maize is gone. Only the bitter cassava are left to survive. So everybody eats garri in the morning and night. The family rots faster than ever because they lo- their love for garri, they love it so much. First, it is her husband-in-law. His knee goes stiff. Then the children start walking on their toes. Then one morning, her mother-in-law couldn't stand up from her stool. You see, cassava carried a hidden poison called cyanide. Grating break it loose, but it needs time to leak into the air and into the water, squeeze out of the sack. And bitter cassava in a drought carries the most. In nineteen eighty-eight in Mozambique, a statistic shows that drought and rot cassava left more than a thousand people unable to walk. So that sole sack in the corner was never a laziness. It was the only safe garri in the compound.
